blocks.text: A 29-year-old woman has received a letter stating that her cervical smear is abnormal. She is worried that she has cancer. Explain the result and the next steps.
Interpret a cervical cytology report showing HSIL and discuss the appropriate management.
A woman has persistent high-risk HPV infection and low-grade cervical cytological changes. Explain how she should be managed.
A patient has atypical glandular cells on cervical cytology. Discuss the investigations required.
Explain the difference between ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL, CIN 1, CIN 2 and CIN 3.
Cervical cytology examines cells collected from the cervix. Abnormalities may reflect HPV infection, precancerous changes, inflammation or, less commonly, invasive malignancy.
Two systems you should understand are:
Bethesda system: used to report cytological abnormalities.
CIN grading: used to describe cervical intraepithelial neoplasia on histology.
Do not confuse the two: cytology describes cells in a sample, whereas histology examines tissue architecture.

items: 1. ASC-US — Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance

blocks.text: Minor cellular changes that are more pronounced than normal but insufficient to classify as a definite squamous intraepithelial lesion.
Management: HPV testing and risk-based follow-up, depending on the programme.
Commonly associated with productive HPV infection and mild cellular abnormalities.
Management: HPV status, age and prior results determine whether surveillance or colposcopy is appropriate.
Indicates a greater likelihood of significant precancerous disease, including CIN 2 or CIN 3.
Management: prompt colposcopic assessment and biopsy, with further management based on risk and findings.

items: 4. ASC-H — Atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL

blocks.text: The sample contains atypical cells in which a high-grade lesion cannot be excluded.
Management: colposcopic assessment is generally indicated.
These cells may originate from the endocervix or, depending on the clinical context, the endometrium.
Possible causes include:
Benign reactive changes.
Cervical glandular precancer.
Adenocarcinoma in situ.
Invasive cervical adenocarcinoma.
Endometrial pathology.

AGC requires appropriate investigation rather than simple reassurance or routine repeat screening. Assessment often includes colposcopy, endocervical sampling and, where indicated by age, bleeding pattern or risk factors, endometrial sampling.
This is a glandular precancerous lesion that requires specialist evaluation and management because of the possibility of associated or underlying invasive disease.
Cytology suspicious for malignancy: urgent diagnostic assessment and tissue diagnosis are required.

subsections.subsection_title: CIN grading: what the examiner expects

blocks.text: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia is a histological diagnosis describing abnormal squamous cells that have not invaded the cervical stroma.
Abnormal cells are largely confined to the lower third of the epithelium.
Often regresses spontaneously, especially in younger patients. Observation is commonly appropriate when invasive disease has been excluded.
Abnormal cells extend into approximately the lower two-thirds of the epithelium in the traditional grading description.
Management depends on age, reproductive goals, pathology review and the risk of progression. Selected patients may undergo surveillance; treatment is common in appropriate cases.
Severe epithelial abnormality involving almost the full thickness or full thickness of the epithelium.
Usually requires treatment, commonly excision, after appropriate evaluation. CIN 3 is not invasive cancer unless stromal invasion is demonstrated.

rows: Often associated with CIN 2 or CIN 3
Glandular precancer; tissue assessment is essential

blocks.text: These associations are not absolute. Cytology and biopsy can disagree, and further evaluation may be needed when clinical suspicion remains high.
If the station asks you to counsel a patient with an abnormal result, first assess what she understands.
Wash your hands.
Introduce yourself and confirm identity.
Ensure privacy.
Ask what she has been told about the result.
Explore her main concern.
Obtain consent to discuss the report and next steps.
Opening statement:

"I understand that receiving an abnormal cervical screening result can be worrying. An abnormal result does not automatically mean cancer. Could you tell me what you have been told so far, and what concerns you most?"
Ask about:
Exact result and date of the test.
Previous HPV tests or cervical cytology.
Previous colposcopy, biopsy or treatment.
Whether she has symptoms such as postcoital bleeding or persistent abnormal discharge.
Pregnancy status, if relevant to management.
Immunosuppression or HIV, where appropriate.
Smoking.
Fertility plans, especially if excisional treatment is being considered.
Important: if the patient reports persistent bleeding or other suspicious symptoms, investigate those symptoms rather than managing her solely through a screening algorithm.

content_groups.group_title: C. Explain the result in plain language

blocks.text: For low-grade changes:

"The sample shows mild changes in the cells on the surface of your cervix. These changes are often associated with HPV and may resolve naturally. We need to follow the recommended pathway to make sure that more significant changes are not present."
For high-grade changes:

"The sample shows more significant cell changes. This does not by itself prove that you have cancer, but it means we need to examine the cervix more closely and may need a biopsy to establish the exact diagnosis."
For glandular abnormalities:
"The sample contains unusual glandular cells. These can have several causes, and we need further investigations to determine where the changes are coming from and whether treatment is needed."

subsections.subsection_title: Management of an abnormal cervical smear

blocks.text: Management is risk-based. The same cytology result may lead to different actions depending on HPV results, age, previous findings and the local screening protocol.

items: Review cytology grade, HPV result, age, symptoms and previous history

blocks.text: Programme-directed surveillance or repeat HPV-based testing where appropriate.
Colposcopy, biopsy and specialist-directed treatment where indicated.

items: Ensure results are communicated and follow-up is completed

content_groups.group_title: B. Practical approach to common results

rows: Routine screening according to the programme, unless symptoms or history require further assessment
HPV status and prior history guide surveillance or colposcopy
Prompt colposcopy and biopsy or other guideline-directed management
Colposcopy and appropriate endocervical evaluation; endometrial assessment when indicated
Specialist assessment and diagnostic excision or other management as appropriate

blocks.text: These are general principles, not a replacement for the applicable national guideline. In some established screening systems, selected high-risk patients may be offered expedited excisional treatment without a preceding biopsy confirming CIN 2 or CIN 3, after careful risk assessment and shared decision-making. This is not appropriate for every patient.
Colposcopy is a magnified examination of the cervix used to investigate abnormal screening results and guide biopsy.
The clinician may:
Insert a speculum and visualise the cervix.
Apply dilute acetic acid.
Assess acetowhite areas, lesion margins, vascular patterns and the transformation zone.
Apply additional solutions where appropriate.
Take directed biopsies of suspicious areas.
Perform endocervical sampling when indicated and appropriate.
Explain when results will be available and the follow-up plan.

A colposcopic appearance can suggest the severity of a lesion but cannot always distinguish high-grade precancer from invasive cancer. Histopathology remains essential when tissue diagnosis is required.
Normal tissue or benign changes.
CIN 1.
CIN 2.
CIN 3.
Glandular precancer, including AIS.
Invasive carcinoma.
An inadequate or discordant result requiring further assessment.
May be appropriate for selected low-grade lesions and selected CIN 2 cases, depending on age, pregnancy status, reproductive priorities, risk and reliability of follow-up.
Examples include:
LLETZ/LEEP: removal of the transformation zone using a wire loop.
Cone biopsy: removal of a cone-shaped section of the cervix, particularly useful when glandular disease, microinvasion or the need for assessment of excision margins is a concern.
Selected eligible lesions may be treated using ablative techniques if the transformation zone and lesion are adequately visualised, invasive disease has been excluded and programme criteria are met.

Cervical abnormalities during pregnancy require pregnancy-specific management. Colposcopy and biopsy may be performed when indicated, but treatment of precancer is generally deferred until after pregnancy unless invasive cancer is suspected. Endocervical curettage is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Excisional treatment, especially repeated or deeper cervical excisions, is associated with an increased risk of adverse obstetric outcomes, including preterm birth. Discuss this risk without exaggerating it, and balance it against the risk posed by untreated disease.

subsections.subsection_title: When should you suspect invasive cancer?

blocks.text: Consider invasive cervical cancer when there is:
A friable, irregular or ulcerated cervical mass.
Persistent or recurrent postcoital bleeding.
Persistent watery or blood-stained discharge.
Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding.
Cytology suspicious for malignancy.
Biopsy evidence of stromal invasion.
Symptoms suggesting advanced disease, such as urinary obstruction, persistent pelvic pain or fistula formation.
Do not wait for a repeat screening test when clinical examination or symptoms raise concern for invasive cancer.

subsections.subsection_title: Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. Does an abnormal cervical smear mean cancer?
No. Most abnormal results represent HPV infection or precancerous changes. Further assessment establishes the severity and determines whether treatment is needed.
Q2. What is the difference between LSIL and HSIL?
LSIL generally indicates low-grade cellular changes, often associated with productive HPV infection. HSIL indicates a greater likelihood of significant precancerous disease such as CIN 2 or CIN 3.
Q3. What is the difference between CIN 3 and invasive cervical cancer?
CIN 3 involves severe epithelial abnormalities without stromal invasion. Invasive cancer penetrates the basement membrane into cervical stroma.
Q4. Why is HPV testing useful in ASC-US?

It helps stratify risk. A negative high-risk HPV test usually indicates a lower risk of significant HPV-related cervical disease than a positive test, although previous history and the local pathway still matter.
Q5. Why are glandular abnormalities important?
They can reflect cervical glandular precancer or malignancy and may occasionally indicate endometrial pathology. They require appropriate assessment rather than routine reassurance.
Q6. What is LLETZ?

Large loop excision of the transformation zone is a procedure that removes abnormal cervical tissue using an electrically heated wire loop. It provides tissue for histopathological assessment and can treat appropriate precancerous lesions.
Q7. Can CIN 2 or CIN 3 regress?

Regression is possible, particularly for some CIN 2 lesions. CIN 3 has a greater risk of progression and is generally treated. Management depends on the patient's circumstances and the relevant guideline.
Q8. Can a patient with abnormal cytology be managed during pregnancy?

Yes. Appropriate colposcopic assessment can be undertaken when indicated. Treatment is generally deferred until after pregnancy unless cancer is suspected, in which case specialist assessment is required.
Q9. What are the complications of cervical excisional treatment?
Bleeding, infection, cervical stenosis and an increased risk of preterm birth, particularly after deeper or repeated excisions.
Q10. What should you do if the smear is abnormal but the cervix looks normal?
Follow the risk-based screening pathway. A normal-looking cervix does not exclude precancerous disease, but an abnormal smear alone does not establish invasive cancer.
Equating HSIL with confirmed invasive cancer.
Confusing cytological terminology with histological CIN grades.
Failing to ask about previous screening results and HPV status.
Forgetting pregnancy and fertility wishes when planning treatment.
Giving a universal repeat interval without identifying the applicable guideline.
Reassuring a patient with persistent bleeding solely because her smear is normal.
Failing to explain why colposcopy or biopsy is required.
Neglecting the importance of communicating results and ensuring follow-up.
Treating CIN 1, CIN 2 and CIN 3 identically.
Failing to investigate glandular abnormalities appropriately.
A — Atypical cells: ASC-US or ASC-H.
L — Low-grade squamous lesion: LSIL.
H — High-grade squamous lesion: HSIL.
G — Glandular abnormalities: AGC or AIS.
R — Review the exact report.
I — Integrate HPV status, symptoms and prior history.
S — Select surveillance, colposcopy or treatment according to risk.
K — Keep track of follow-up until the pathway is completed.
Abnormal cytology is not the same as invasive cancer.
HSIL carries a greater likelihood of significant precancer than LSIL.
CIN is a histological diagnosis; cytology alone cannot determine stromal invasion.
Glandular abnormalities require appropriate investigation.
Symptoms suspicious for cancer require diagnostic assessment regardless of the screening result.
A 31-year-old woman has a cervical cytology result showing HSIL. She is asymptomatic and wishes to have children in the future.
Which is the most appropriate next step?
Reassure her that HSIL is benign and no follow-up is necessary.
Arrange appropriate colposcopic assessment and discuss biopsy and subsequent management, including fertility considerations.
Diagnose invasive cervical cancer without further investigations.
Recommend hysterectomy immediately in every case.
